title: Defects in long-chain 3-hydroxy acyl-CoA dehydrogenase lead to hepatocellular carcinoma: A novel etiology of hepatocellular carcinoma.

Novelty and Impact: 
Dysregulated fatty acid oxidation is implicated in development of hepatocellular 
carcinoma (HCC). For the first time, we established a mouse model with an LCHAD 
defect that results in development of hepatic steatosis at younger age and HCC without 
cirrhosis in the older population. Proteomic analysis on liver of animals with LCHAD 
defect revealed altered expression of early cancer markers. This novel finding indicates 
that LCHAD defects predispose to HCC and documents that mitochondrial dysfunction 
plays an important role in the pathogenesis of HCC. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.


 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
ABSTRACT  
The incidence of both nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) and hepatocellular 
carcinoma (HCC) have been increasing at an alarming rate. Little is known about NAFLD 
without cirrhosis as a risk for HCC. Here we report, for the first time, generation of a 
mouse model with a defect in long chain 3-hydoxy acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (LCHAD). 
The LCHAD exon 15 deletion was embryonic lethal to the homozygous mice whereas 
heterozygous mice (HT) develop significant hepatic steatosis starting at young age (3 
months old) and HCC at older age (>13 months old) without any evidence of fibrosis or 
cirrhosis. None of the wild-type (WT) mice developed steatosis and HCC (n=39), whereas 
HT-LCHAD mice (n=41) showed steatosis and ~20% (8/41) developed liver masses with 
histological features of HCC. Proteomic analysis on liver tissues from WT- and HT- mice 
with no signs of HCC was conducted. Proteins with significant changes in abundance 
were identified by mass spectrometry. Abundance of twenty-four proteins was 
significantly different (p<0.01) between WT and HT-LCHAD mice. The proteins found to 
This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.


 
 
vary in abundance are associated with different cellular response processes ranging from 
intermediary metabolism of carbohydrate, protein, and lipid to oxidative stress, signal 
transduction and the process of tumorigenesis. Protein expression pattern of the HT-
LCHAD mouse liver indicates predisposition to HCC and suggests that impaired hepatic 
mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation plays an important role in development and progression 
of HCC. To assess the implication of these studies in human disease, we demonstrated 
significant downregulation of HADHA transcripts in HCC patients. 
 
 
1. Introduction  
Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is a cause of cancer-related deaths worldwide1, 2. In the 
past 15 years, the incidence of HCC has doubled, becoming a major public health 
concern. Current treatment options, such as locoregional therapy, surgical resection and 
liver transplantation offer marginal clinical benefits due to late diagnosis. The cytotoxic 
systemic therapy also does not work well due to chemo-resistance in HCC3. The 
development of effective therapeutic strategies for HCCs require improving our 
understanding of molecular mechanisms involved in HCC development and progression. 
The etiology of HCC varies in different parts of the world. Chronic Hepatitis B virus (HBV) 
infection, hepatitis C Virus (HCV) infection, alcohol abuse, alcoholic and nonalcoholic fatty 
liver diseases (AFLD and NAFLD) are mainly responsible for development of HCC4.  
This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.


 
 
However, the pathogenic promoters of HCC are shifting from viral and alcohol related 
liver disease to obesity, type 2 diabetes, and NAFLD5, 6. The worrisome part of these risk 
factors is that they are largely spread in general population and are more likely linked to 
HCC associated with non-cirrhotic livers7, 8. NAFLD, which is characterized by excess fat 
in the liver, progresses from simple steatosis to nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), and 
can further progress to cirrhosis in a significant number of people9, 10. The number of 
individuals with NAFLD, potentially at risk of developing HCC is likely much larger than 
imagined. Thus, rapidly growing literature is focused on development of HCC in NAFLD 
patients without cirrhosis7, 8. This demands urgent need to understand the risk factors 
linked to the development of HCC in steatotic, non-cirrhotic livers.  
Although a growing literature has documented the clinical relevance between NAFLD and 
HCC development, the molecular mechanisms underlying NAFLD-related HCC 
carcinogenesis remains unknown. Work published by our group and others have 
documented an important role of mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation in development of 
NAFLD11, 12.  For example, mitochondria play a central role in cellular energy homeostasis 
and mitochondrial dysfunction with impaired fatty acid oxidation leads to accumulation of 
reactive oxygen species (ROS), which in turn contributes to malignant transformation and 
tumor promotion. Thus, uncovering the specific regulatory pathways may shed new light 
on our understanding of the underlying molecular pathways involved in NAFLD-HCC 
related tumorigenesis and potentially may lead to identification of therapeutic targets.  
This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.


 
 
Defects in mitochondrial fatty acid β-oxidation are known to cause hepatic steatosis 
without progression to cirrhosis in murine models12, 13. The first step of β-oxidation of long-
chain fatty acids is catalyzed by acyl-CoA dehydrogenase followed by three steps 
catalyzed by a complex mitochondrial trifunctional protein (MTP). MTP is a hetero-
octamer, composed of four α and four β subunits14. The α subunit contains the activities 
of the long-chain enoyl-CoA hydratase and LCHAD, which catalyze the second and third 
steps of long chain mitochondrial β-oxidation. The β subunit contains the activity of long-
chain -3-ketoacyl-CoA thiolase, which catalyzes the last step of long chain fatty acid 
mitochondrial β-oxidation. 
Human genes encoding for α (HADHA) and β (HADHB) subunits are localized to 
chromosome 2 (2p23) 15, 16. The LCHAD protein is a reported synonym for the human 
gene HADHA that encodes alpha subunit of trifunctional multienzyme complex. LCHAD 
deficiency, with normal activity of the other two trifunctional protein enzymes, is the most 
frequent of the recessively inherited MTP defects15-18. The most common mutation 
causing LCHAD deficiency is the G1528C mutation in exon 15 of the HADHA gene. Exon 
15 codes for a region in α subunit that contains the active site of the LCHAD 
enzyme.  Patients with LCHAD deficiency present during infancy with hypoglycemic coma 
and hepatic steatosis. Other manifestations include cardiomyopathy, recurrent 
rhabdomyolysis, peripheral neuropathy and chorioretinopathy19. Mothers carrying fetuses 
with LCAHD deficiency may develop acute fatty liver of pregnancy20, 21. Little is known 
This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.


 
 
about the phenotype associated with heterozygosity for an LCHAD defect and the risk for 
NAFLD and HCC in the heterozygous adult population. 
Here we report, for the first time, development of a novel mouse model for a LCHAD 
defect in exon 15 of the HADHA gene. The homozygous defect is embryonic lethal, 
whereas heterozygous mice develop hepatic steatosis at younger age and HCC without 
cirrhosis at older age. We conducted proteomics analyses to characterize the protein 
expression patterns of the heterozygous LCHAD mouse liver with a predisposition to 
HCC. More importantly, without knowing heterozygosity for LCHAD in the HCC patient 
population, we demonstrated significant reduction in HADHA transcript in HCC patients. 
Our studies provide important insights into the role of impaired mitochondrial fatty acid 
oxidation in the development of HCC without cirrhosis.  
 
2. Materials and Methods  
2.1 Transgenic Mice Studies 
2.1.1. Generation of LCHAD deficient mouse model 
A knockout mouse model was generated with a defect in the LCHAD gene by deletion in 
Exon 15. A 6.2 kb fragment of the mouse genomic DNA encoding for exon 15 and its 
flanking intronic sequences of the α-subunit was sub cloned into a pGEM-3Z vector (Cat 
# P2151) from Promega (Madison, WI), and this plasmid was used as a template to create 
This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.


 
 
the long arm and the short arms of the targeting construct. An 809 bp fragment upstream 
of exon 15 was cloned out of the pGEM-3Z vector to serve as the short arm of the 
construct and was inserted into a pPNT vector using the Hind III restriction site. Likewise, 
a 2.9 kb fragment downstream of exon 15 was cloned out to serve as the long arm and 
was also inserted into the pPNT vector using the Xho 1 and Not 1 restriction sites as 
shown in Figure 1A. A pPNT vector containing a neomycin phophotransferase gene (Neo) 
and herpes simplex virus thymidine kinase (HSV-TK) expression cassettes that served 
as both the replacement gene and the selection marker, was used to transfect SV129 
embryonic stem cells via electroporation. Positive recombinant stem cells were injected 
into blastocysts that were implanted into psuedopregnant mice to produce chimeric mice. 
Chimeric mice were then mated to C57Bl/6 mice to produce the F1 generation. F1 
generation mice were mated to breed succeeding generations.  
Only male mice were used in this study as they exhibited the phenotypes observed. Mice 
were maintained and bred at the University of Missouri-Columbia animal facility under a 
14/10 hour light/dark cycle. Mice were housed using ventilated racks and cages from 
Allentown (Allentown, NJ) with 1/8” corn cob beddings from The Andersen’s (Maumee, 
OH) with aspen shavings from Nepco (Warrensburg, NY) changed at least once per 
week. Breeding mice were fed with 11% fat (5015) from Lab diet (PMI International St. 
Louis MO) while non-breeding mice were fed with 6.5% fat (5008) also from Lab diet. All 
mice were provided filtered drinking water ad libitum.

The study had a formal approval from the Wake Forest University School of Medicine and 
University of Missouri-Columbia and the care of the animals was in accordance with the 
Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee guidelines of Wake Forest University 
School of Medicine and University of Missouri-Columbia. 
2.1.2. Genotyping and DNA analysis  
For genotyping, tail clips from weaned 21-day old mice were used to isolate DNA using a 
DNeasy Tissue Kit (Quigen, Germantown, MD) and genotyping was done.  (See 
Supplementary file).  
2.1.3. Tissue collection 
Mice were euthanized using a CO2 chamber. Liver tissues were collected and fixed in 
10% formalin for normal histology and fat staining. Extra tissues were snap frozen in liquid 
nitrogen or embedded in embedding medium (Tissue-Tek OCT Compound 4583) from 
Sakura Finetek USA Inc. (Torrance, CA), snap frozen and stored at -70°C until further 
use. 
2.1.4. Histological analysis 
Tissues sections mounted on slides were analyzed for cellular morphology and structure 
by staining with Hematoxylin and Eosin (H & E). Tissues were trimmed to less than 3mm 
in thickness, embedded in paraffin, sectioned at 4 μm, and stained with hematoxylin and 
eosin. Oil-Red-O staining (Hartmann-Leddon Co., Philadelpia, PA) was done to assess 
fatty infiltration in liver sections.  Tissues used to detect the presence of fat were quick-
This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.


 
 
frozen, cryostatically sectioned at 4 μm and stained with Oil- Red-O.  For the assessment 
of hepatic steatosis, histopathologic criteria proposed by Brunt et. al. was adopted22 (See 
Supplementary file). 
2.2. Biochemical analysis 
2.2.1. Tissue triglyceride measurement 
Fresh Liver tissues obtained at the time of sacrifice were used for the measurement of 
triglycerides. Lipids were extracted from approximately 30-100 mg minced liver by the 
chloroform/methanol method as previously described by Frayn and Maycock23.  
2.2.2. Hepatic Mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation measurement 
Mitochondria were isolated from fresh liver samples as described previously24. The 
oxidation of fatty acids in the mitochondria was measured by 14CO2 generated from 
complete combustion of 14C palmitate (American Radiochemicals)25 (See Supplementary 
file).   
2.3. Proteomics Studies 
2.3.1. Sample preparation 
Three WT and three HT-LCHAD mice without cancerous lesions were sacrificed at the 
age of 13 to 18 months. Liver tissues were collected, snap frozen and stored at -70°C until 
use. Frozen liver samples were pulverized in liquid nitrogen using mortar and pestle and  
whole cell lysates were prepared (See Supplementary file).  
2.3.2. Two dimensional polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (2D-PAGE) 
This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.


 
 
Aliquots of whole cell lysates containing 700µg of protein were separated in the first 
dimension by application on to 24 cm, pH 3–10 nonlinear IPG strips and separated in the 
second dimension using 10-18% SDS-PAGE gels (See Supplementary file).   
2.3.3. Data acquisition and analysis 
To detect significant differences in the abundance of proteins between WT and HT-
LCHAD mice, three gel images from each category were imported and were analyzed 
using ImageMaster Platinum v.6 system from GE healthcare after normalization (See 
Supplementary file).  
2.3.4. Protein Identification by Mass Spectrometry  
Protein spots showing significant difference in expression (p <0.01) were cut from multiple 
gels, digested with trypsin using a standard in-gel digestion protocol (Trypsin, modified, 
sequencing grade, Promega, Madison, WI, USA) 26 and analyzed by LCMS + MS/MS 
using an LTQ Orbitrap coupled with a Proxeon Easy nLC (See Supplementary file). 
2.4. SDS-PAGE and Western blotting 
Liver tissues of WT, HT-LCHAD mice W/O any cancer and cancerous tissue from HT-
LCHAD mice liver W/Cancer lesions, were  lysed with RIPA buffer. Proteins in the lysates 
were separated by Laemmli’s SDS-PAGE27 and identified by western blotting (See 
Supplementary file).  
2.5. cDNA array study of HCC patients 
This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.


 
 
Origene (Rockville, MD, USA) TissueScan Liver Cancer cDNA Array (Cat# LVRT101) 
was utilized to assess HADHA transcript using the manufacturer’s protocol. The plate 
contained cDNAs from eight normal and twenty-six liver cancer tissues. Ready to use 
specific forward and reverse primers and a custom RT2 qPCR Primer Assay (cat. no. 
330001, Qiagen) was created to measure HADHA transcripts. PCR was performed in a 
thermocycler (Roche, Madison, WI, USA) using the qSTAR SYBR Master Mix Kit (Bio 
Rad). The following cycling conditions were used: 3 min at 95 °C; 50 cycles: 10 s at 
95 °C; 30 s at 56 °C; 15 s at 72 °C with additional 7 min at 72 °C  and then cooling 
down. For every PCR run, control reactions performed in the absence of template for 
each primer pair and these were consistently negative. Amplicon sizing and relative 
quantitation were performed by the manufacturer’s software. qPCR data were analyzed 
using the comparative 2^(-ΔΔCt) method and transcript levels were normalized to β-
actin and expressed as fold-control patients. 
2.6. Statistical analysis 
All analyses were carried out using GraphPad Prism version 4 for Windows (GraphPad 
Software San Diego California USA, www.graphpad.com). Data is expressed as mean + 
SD. Statistical significance was determined with Student t-test. A p-value < 0.05 was 
considered statistically significant. To determine statistical differences in mean HADHA 
transcript levels between HCC and control patients, a two-tailed student’s t-test was 
performed (p value = 0.002).

3. Results     
3.1. Generation of LCHAD KO mice and molecular Characterization 
A targeting vector, with a neomycin and HSV-TK expression cassettes, was used to 
replace exon 15 and its flanking 5’ and 3’ intronic regions of the mouse HADHA gene 
utilizing homologous recombination in 129 SVEV ES cells (Figure 1A). This deleted a 2.1 
kb region and created a defect in the LCHAD gene that codes for the active site and 
induced a state of LCHAD deficiency. Injection of recombinant ES cells into blastocysts 
and 
implantation 
into 
pseudopregnant 
mice 
resulted 
in 
Chimeric 
mice 
(C57BL6/SVEV129). Mating of chimeric mice to C57BL6 mice produced agouti pups. The 
heterozygous F1 generation were intercrossed.  Heterozygote mating produced only wild 
type (LCHAD+/+) and heterozygous (LCHAD+/-) mice. No homozygous mice (LCHAD-/-) 
were produced in all HT/HT mating. The genotypes were confirmed by Southern blots, 
which showed the loss of exon 15 and the presence of Neo gene in LCHAD+/- mice (Figure 
1B and 1C).  
Western blot analysis of proteins isolated from the liver using polyclonal α-subunit 
antibody showed no significant difference in the expression of the α-subunit (LCHAD) in 
WT and HT-LCHAD mice(Figure 1D and 1E). β-subunit and short chain 3-hydroxy acyl

Co-A dehydrogenase (SCHAD) antibodies were also used for comparison with no 
significant difference in expression between WT and HT mice (Figure 1D and 1E). 
These results document that deletion of exon 15 in the MTPα subunit, which contains 
the catalytic site of the LCHAD enzyme, did not impact expression of the mitochondrial 
trifunctional protein subunits. 
3.2. LCHAD heterozygous mice develop hepatic steatosis at young age 
Histopathological analysis on H & E stained liver sections was performed. A mixed 
microvesicular and macrovesicular steatosis was observed in liver sections from HT-
LCHAD mice compared to WT mice (Figure 2A, top panel a). Oil-Red-O staining 
confirmed the steatosis observed in the H and E slides and showed little or no fatty 
infiltration in WT mice while there was considerable fat infiltration in HT-LCHAD mice 
(Figure 2A, bottom panel b). Mounted tissue sections of other organs were also tested 
but they did not show fatty infiltration in either WT or HT-LCHAD mice (pictures not 
shown). For assessing hepatic steatosis, histopathologic criteria proposed by Brunt et.al. 
22 was adopted in scoring H and E slides. HT-LCHAD mice exhibit moderate steatosis, 
scored at 1.5 (SD = + 0.5, n=10) compared to WT mice, scored at 0.5 (SD = + 0.34, n=10) 
and the scores were significantly different (p=0.05). 
Liver triglycerides levels were significantly elevated in HT-LCHAD mice, 57.53 mg TG/mg 
wet liver (SD = + 12.33, n=3) compared to WT mice 12.26 mg TG/mg wet liver (SD = + 
This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.


 
 
0.36, n=3) and the difference is statistically significant (p<0.05) confirming the observed 
steatosis in HT-LCHAD mice (Figure 2B).  
Mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation as assessed by measuring the levels of radiolabeled 
14C CO2 produced as the by-product of complete oxidation of radiolabeled  1-14C palmitate 
in isolated mitochondria from liver tissue showed significantly marked reduction in 
palmitate oxidation (p<0.05) indicative of reduced mitochondrial LCHAD enzymatic 
activity between WT and HT-LCHAD mice (Figure 2C).  
3.3. LCHAD heterozygous mice develop HCC at old age without cirrhosis: 
To characterize the phenotype at older age, eighty animals including 41 HT-LCHAD and 
39 WT-mice, 13-18 months of age were sacrificed. Around 20% of HT-LCHAD mice (8/41) 
showed mass lesions in the liver, whereas none of the WT mice had mass lesions in the 
liver (Figure 3A). The hepatic tissues in the HT-LCHAD mice develop multiple HCC 
nodules and the size of nodules varied from 3-10 mm in diameter giving irregular surface 
contour to the liver (Figure 3B). Histological analysis revealed changes consistent with 
HCC including trabecular pattern, small cell changes, cytologic atypia, mitotic activity, 
absence of Kupffer cells, and the loss of the reticulin network but there was no  evidence 
of inflammation or fibrosis in HT-LCHAD animals (Figure 3C).  
3.4. Proteomic Analysis: Differential expression of proteins in the liver of WT and 
HT- LCHAD mice: 
This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.


 
 
Frozen liver samples from three WT and three HT-LCHAD mice were analyzed by two-
dimensional polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (2D-PAGE) and separated proteins of 
significance were identified by LCMS/MS/MS using LTQ-Orbitrap-XL. Staining of gels 
with colloidal Coomassie Brilliant Blue G 250 displayed an average of 650 resolved 
proteins with isoelectric pH (pIs) between 3 and 10 (Fig 4A). Spot volumes (area x 
intensity) was used as a measure of protein expression or abundance. Spots that showed 
more than 1.5 fold increase or 0.5 fold decrease in abundance were included in the 
analysis and proteins that were present in sufficient amounts were selected for 
identification by mass spectrometry (Table S1). Comparison of 2D patterns of liver lysates 
from WT and HT-LCHAD mice revealed 95% of protein spots matching and only 5% of 
protein spots were expressed differently. Expression of only twenty four protein spots was 
significantly different (p< 0.01). Five of the twenty four proteins were increased in 
abundance in HT-LCHAD as compared to WT mice whereas remaining nineteen proteins 
were decreased in abundance. These twenty four protein spots with significant difference 
in abundance were selected for protein identification by mass spectrometry using LTQ-
Orbitrap-XL. More than one protein was identified in most of the spots, but only top hit 
protein identification from each spot with at least 25% sequence coverage and 5 unique 
peptides was included in the results as summarized in Table S1 and depicted in Figure 
4B. The upregulated proteins identified in the present study are mainly involved in 
molecular and cellular processes like growth, proliferation and stress. On the contrary, 
This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.


 
 
the downregulated proteins are involved in energy metabolism (Glycolysis/OXPHOS), 
lipid and protein metabolism, signal transduction and tumor suppression (Table S1). 
Table S2 summarizes the involvement of some identified proteins in the regulation of 
cellular activities and development of HCC and other cancers. 
3.5. Validation of 2D-PAGE/Mass Spectrometry data 
In order to validate the results obtained from 2D-PAGE/mass spectrometry analyses and 
to investigate the possibility of identified proteins becoming relevant biomarkers for HCC, 
western blot analysis was performed using specific primary antibodies.  Selection of 
proteins was done on the basis of their relevance to present investigation and strong 
correlation with HCC and other cancers.  Four proteins that are upregulated and one 
protein that is downregulated in liver lysates of HT-LCHAD mouse were selected for 
validation (Figure S1 and Table S1). Protein samples prepared from same three HT-
LCHAD and WT mice liver tissues were run on SDS-polyacrylamide gel and analyzed by 
western blotting.  The western blotting results confirmed our 2D findings and showed that 
TRAP1, GAPDH, GMPS, and Hsp70 were expressed in significantly increased amounts 
in HT-LCHAD mice whereas expression of CCS was decreased (Figure 5A).  
3.6. Expression of identified cancer targets in HT-LCHAD mice with cancer lesions 
(HT-C)

Out of five proteins selected for validation, expression of only three proteins TRAP1, 
GAPDH, and CCS was followed in HT-LCHAD mice that developed cancer lesions (HT-
C) by SDS-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis and western blotting. Limited supply of 
liver tissues from HT-C mice made us analyze protein expression by only 1-dimensional 
electrophoresis as opposed to 2-dimensional electrophoresis/MS analysis. Selections of 
three targets was based on more than 2-fold increase or less than 0.5-fold decrease in 
expression of proteins in HT-LCHAD mice as compared to WT mice as noticed in western 
blotting. All three targets in LCHAD HT-C follow the same pattern of up- or down-
expression as reported in HT-LCHAD without cancer (Figure 5B), but to little bit different 
extent because of different animals used for the analysis.  
3.7. HADHA expression in HCC patients 
To assess significance of LCHAD in HCC, we examined HADHA mRNA transcripts in 
controls and HCC tissues utilizing cDNAs from eight normal and twenty-six liver cancer 
tissues. A significant downregulation of HADHA transcripts as compared to controls was 
noted (p=0.002) (Fig. 6). 
4. Discussion 
The uncontrolled growth and proliferation of cancer cells constantly requires continuous 
supply of macromolecular building blocks and energy and they meet these demands by 
altering their metabolic pathways. Such reprograming of metabolic pathways is the 
hallmark of cancer cells. The best understood metabolic alteration in cancer cells is 
This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.


 
 
enhanced glycolysis (the Warburg effect) despite of normal oxygen tension. In addition to 
altered glucose metabolism, there is dysregulated FA metabolism in cancer cells. 
Increased cellular proliferation, a common feature of all cancers, is accomplished by 
increasing de-novo synthesis of FA, decreasing the rate of FA degradation, and 
increasing FA release from lipid storage. Enormous amount of data is available to support 
role of elevated de novo synthesis of FA and dysregulated FA oxidation (FAO) in 
malignancies. However, there is disagreement on to whether up- or down-regulation of 
FAO is involved in HCC progression. This discrepancy in up-or downregulation of FAO in 
HCC patients may reflect in part the tumor heterogeneity of HCC.  Whatever is the 
association of HCC with FAO, there is increased evidence pointing towards targeting FAO 
to treat HCC28. In this regard, in the present investigation, we have established a novel 
mouse model to assess role of FAO in the progression of HCC without cirrhosis.  
A novel finding in our study is the development of HCC in HT- LCHAD mice. Our mouse 
model with a defect in LCHAD develops HCC in the setting of hepatic steatosis without 
cirrhosis, which offers unique opportunity to study the underlying molecular pathways 
leading to development of HCC due to defects in mitochondrial β-oxidation. Results 
demonstrate that LCHAD deficiency has important implications. The absence of 
homozygous pups in our model implies the importance of intact long-chain fatty acid 
oxidation in embryonic/fetal development. Our previous studies in MTP knockout mice 
with absent MTPα subunit documented that intact mitochondrial long chain fatty acid 
This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.


 
 
oxidation is essential for fetal development, and its absence causes intra uterine growth 
retardation11. Another important phenotypic feature of our model is that heterozygosity for 
an LCHAD defect causes NAFLD in young mice without evidence of inflammation or 
cirrhosis. Importantly, deletion of exon 15, the catalytic site of LCHAD in the MTP-α 
subunit, did not alter expression of the MTP-α and -β subunits. However, it reduced 
hepatic fatty acid oxidation, leading to development of hepatic steatosis. This provides 
further insight into understanding the role of genetic susceptibility for NAFLD and the 
possible role of fatty acid oxidation in the pathogenesis of NAFLD. Interestingly, the 
development of HCC appears to be unique to the LCHAD mouse model among other fatty 
acid oxidation disorders. Development of HCC was not reported in other mouse models 
for fatty acid oxidation disorders, such as very long chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase 
deficiency29 or long chain acyl Co-A dehydrogenase deficiency consistent with clinical 
heterogeneity and a genotype-phenotype correlation in fatty acid oxidation disorders17, 30.  
In order to assess molecular changes in older HT-LCHAD population that may lead to 
HCC, we performed proteome analysis.  
Proteomics is not only useful in biomarker and drug discovery but also helps in 
understanding the molecular processes underlying cancer progression, metastasis, and 
recurrence. This is the first report of protein profiling in a mouse model with defective 
mitochondrial LCHAD enzyme, which develops cancerous lesions in liver without 
underlying cirrhosis. We revealed that expression of twenty-four proteins (almost 5% of 
This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.


 
 
total proteome) is consistently different and highly significant (p<.01) in WT and HT-
LCHAD mice liver that has no signs of HCC (Table S1). The proteins found to vary in 
abundance are part of several different cellular response processes ranging from 
intermediary metabolism of carbohydrate, protein, and lipid to oxidative stress, signal 
transduction and process of tumorigenesis. Increased abundance of Glyceraldehyde-3-
phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH), GMP Synthase (GMPS), Heat shock protein 9A or 
stress-70 protein (Hsp70), and TNF receptor associated protein 1 (TRAP1) along with 
decreased abundance of copper chaperone for superoxide dismutase (CCS1) are 
discussed in detail because of their strong correlation with development of HCC and other 
malignancies. 
GAPDH is an enzyme of Glycolysis and catalyzes conversion of Glyceraldehyde 3-P to 
1,3-biphosphoglycerate.  Increased abundance of GAPDH, as observed in HT-LCHAD 
liver, is also reported in renal cell carcinoma, lung, breast, prostate cancers, HBV and 
HCV-associated HCC31. Increased glucose metabolism, a prominent biochemical 
signature and metabolic phenotype of most solid tumors and long known in case of liver 
tumors, plays an important role in several biosynthetic processes facilitating uncontrolled 
growth. Furthermore, a strong link between GAPDH up-regulation and c-Jun, a proto-
oncogene involved in liver tumorigenesis has been reported32.   
GMPS, an enzyme of de novo purine biosynthesis, converts xanthine monophosphate to 
guanine monophosphate and uses glutamine as amido-N-donor. Up regulation of GMPS

is reported in normal rapidly proliferating cells and cancer cells33. Several genomic studies 
revealed amplification of GMPS gene in multiple cancers33. GMPS is required and 
regulates activity of histone H2B deubiquitylation enzyme USP7 in Drosophila and human 
cells through an allosteric mechanism. Recently, Human USP7 (a.k.a. HAUSP) has been 
reported as modulator of the p53 tumor suppressor pathway, though role of GMPS in this 
regulation is still not known33. Moreover, GMPS is revealed as the repression target of 
p53 in HCC, and its upregulation results in disruption of tumor-suppressive p53 pathway 
in liver cancer34.  
HSPs, which are induced in response to cellular stress are highly conserved molecular 
chaperone proteins, identified to enhance the cell proliferation, invasion, survival, and 
metastasis in a wide variety of human cancers. Because tumor cells are continuously 
challenged by constant stress conditions in their microenvironment, overexpression of 
HSP is widely reported in many human cancers, including HCC and is related to their 
aggressive properties35. Many members of HSPs perform their functions by making sure 
proteins are folded correctly, inhibiting their aggregation induced by stress, regulation of 
transcriptional networks and signal transduction pathways35. HSP70 is increased in 
abundance along with HSP27, and HSP90 in HCC and serves as diagnostic and 
prognostic target for HCC35. It has been identified as most abundantly upregulated gene 
in early HCC, and is used as one of the proteins in a panel of three immunohistochemistry 
markers (Glypican 3, HSP70, and Glutamine Synthetase or Glypican 3, HSP70, and

enhancer of zeste homologue2) to distinguish early HCC from high-grade dysplastic 
nodules in both liver biopsies and surgical specimens35. The migration and invasion 
abilities of HCC cells were significantly inhibited by knocking down HSP70, possibly 
because of inhibiting Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway that serve an important role in the 
progression of HCC36. Targeting HSPs with their specific inhibitors is an attractive 
therapeutic approach and promises use of HSPs inhibitors in HCC treatment35.  
TRAP1, a member of HSP90 family, controls a variety of physiological functions, including 
proliferation, differentiation, and survival of cells37. Moreover, recent findings indicated 
role of TRAP1 as a metabolic switch between mitochondrial respiration (OXPHOS) and 
aerobic glycolysis (Warburg effect) as well as in regulation of cancer stem cells (CSCs) 
37.  Kowalik et al utilized a well characterized rat resistant-hepatocyte (R-H) model of 
hepatocarcinogenesis and identified that switch from OXPHOS to glycolysis is a very 
early event in hepatocarcinogenesis, occurs in preneoplastic foci or nodules that develop 
into hepatocellular carcinoma later and is maintained in advanced HCC38. These changes 
in metabolism are restricted to preneoplastic nodule progression to HCC and not noticed 
in non-neoplastic liver regeneration occurring after second/third partial hepatectomy. This 
metabolic shift in glucose utilization is required to face hypoxic conditions that occur in 
the core of a fast growing tumor mass and to sustain metabolic needs of tumor cells38.

mice liver cells that have not yet developed any cancer and possibly are in preneoplastic

WT liver samples did not show complete absence of TRAP1. The absence of TRAP1 in 
2D-PAGE gels of WT mouse thus could be a detection issue due to less sensitive nature 
of Coomassie blue staining used in the present investigation. A much sensitive silver-
staining of the same 2DE gels could have resulted in detection of TRAP1 spot in WT-
mouse, just in agreement with western blotting results. Same fact is true for the other two 
overexpressed proteins GMPS and Cysteine sulfinic acid decarboxylase (CSAD), which 
are also observed to be missing in the 2DE gel of WT mice liver lysates.  
Studies related to metabolism of long chain fatty acids in HCC suggest that there is  
increased  generation of hydrogen peroxide and oxidative stress by increased FAO by 
way of extra mitochondrial pathways (i.e., in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum and in the 
peroxisomes). The ultimate result is alterations in gene expression and in DNA itself 39. 
In a cell, oxidative stress is counteracted by copper-zinc Superoxide dismutase (SOD1) 
and its activating chaperone which is CCS1. Both SOD1 and CCS1 are localized in 
cytosol and mitochondrial intermembrane space and act on superoxide radicals 
generated in mitochondria. SOD1 requires CCS1 for its activity40, 41. In eukaryotic cells, 
reactive oxygen species (ROS) are generated by reduction of oxygen molecule to 
superoxide radicals (O2-), which is very unstable and damaging to cells. In vivo, SOD1 
dismutes O2- into O2 and H2O2. H2O2 also produces more deleterious hydroxyl radicals 
and is removed by catalases and peroxidases. We observed decreased abundance of

CCS1 in HT-LCHAD mouse liver cells, indicative of oxidative stress. However, no 
significant changes were noticed in the abundance of SOD1. Elchuri et al reported that 
deficiency of CuZnSOD in mice leads to persistent oxidative damage contributing to  
development of HCC later in life42. In this regard, decreased abundance of indoleamine-
2,3-dioxygenase (IDO) in the HT-LCHAD liver cells, which uses O2- as oxidizing agent 
also explains accumulation of O2- resulting in oxidative stress microenvironment.   
The overexpression of other targets like CSAD43 and reduced expression of Proliferation 
associated protein 2G4 (PA2G4)44, Nitrilase45, Annexin A646, N-myc downstream- 
regulated gene 2 Protein  (NDRG2)47, Tyrosine 3-monooxygenase/tryptophan 5-
monooxygenase 
activation 
protein/epsilon 
polypeptide48, 
Methylcrotonyl 
CoA 
carboxylase (MCC)49, Catechol-O-methyl transferase (COMT)50 are in good agreement 
with previous data. However, involvement of Cytochrome C oxidase51,  Alpha-
aminoadipic semialdehyde dehydrogenase52, IDO53, and  Arsenite methyl transferase54 
in HCC has not been well documented. Their association with HCC may indicate reduced 
mitochondrial activity, increased oxidative stress, lowered immunosuppressive activity 
and altered methylation of DNA.  
The role of HADHA expression and mutations in the development of HCC has never been 
studied. We observed a significant decrease in HADHA transcript in HCC patients. 
Decreased mRNA levels in HCC could be ascribed to impaired transcription and/or 
increased degradation of transcripts. However, mechanisms that regulate HADHA 
This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.


 
 
transcripts in HCC require further investigation. Together, these results may suggest that 
impairment in the oxidation of long-chain fatty acids due to reduction in HADHA transcript 
may serve a cancer-promoting role in HCC. Future studies are required to assess HADHA 
mutational defects in HCC population. 
Significance of other metabolic disorders could not be ignored in the development of 
HCC, for example, HCC is associated with glycogen storage disease (GSD), another 
recessively inherited metabolic liver disease. Patients with type 1, 3 and 4 GSD have 
been reported to develop HCC55-57. Recent work has linked glucose-6-phosphatase-α 
deficiency to altered inflammatory and tumorigenic responses in the liver. Regulation of 
hepatic STAT3 and NFκB signaling pathways were implicated in GSD type 1a mice 
receiving gene therapy58. Future studies that examine these signaling pathways in our 
mouse model may shed additional light on the underlying mechanisms that link hepatic 
mitochondrial disorders to development and progression of HCC.  
In summary, for the first time, we established reduced HADHA transcript level in HCC 
patients. We further established a novel mouse model of LCHAD deficiency that leads to 
NAFLD in young heterozygous mice and HCC without cirrhosis in the older population. 
Various targets of cancer progression in HT-LCHAD mice illustrate a predisposition to 
HCC. Impaired LCHAD is a new etiology of HCC. This novel mouse model will be of great 
interest to the scientific community-investigating role of FAO in HCC and its treatment.
